quests.title: The House of Wisdom

skill.name: Baghdad and the House of Wisdom
skill.subject: history

quests.story: Welcome to Baghdad, around AD 900, one of the biggest cities in the world! Step inside the House of Wisdom, where scholars share books and big ideas.
quests.instruction: Read each question about Baghdad, then tap the right book.
quests.hint: Think about a great city of learning on a river, where scholars collected knowledge from many lands.

questions.ask: Which caliph founded the city of Baghdad in AD 762?
questions.fact: He chose a spot on the River Tigris where important trade routes met.

questions.ask: What shape was al-Mansur's first city of Baghdad?
questions.fact: The Round City had four gates, with the caliph's palace and a mosque at its centre.

questions.ask: Which river does Baghdad stand beside?
questions.fact: Boats on the Tigris brought goods from as far away as India and China.

questions.ask: What was the House of Wisdom in Baghdad?
questions.fact: Scholars of different faiths worked there together, studying and sharing ideas.

questions.ask: Into which language did scholars translate Greek and Persian books?
questions.fact: Many ancient Greek books survived because they were copied into Arabic.

questions.ask: Which mathematician's name gave us the word 'algorithm'?
questions.fact: His book also gave us the word 'algebra', from the Arabic 'al-jabr'.

questions.ask: Which useful material did Baghdad learn to make from China?
questions.fact: Paper mills opened in Baghdad in the late 700s, so books became cheaper to make.

questions.ask: Which instrument helped scholars measure the positions of the stars?
questions.fact: Astrolabes also helped people tell the time and find the direction of Mecca for prayer.

questions.ask: Who could be cared for in Baghdad's large hospitals?
questions.fact: Hospitals had separate wards and trained doctors, and treatment was often free.

questions.ask: Which great trade route linked Baghdad with China?
questions.fact: Merchants carried silk, spices, paper and new ideas along the Silk Road.

questions.ask: Which family of caliphs ruled from Baghdad?
questions.fact: Abbasid caliphs ruled from Baghdad for about 500 years.

questions.ask: Which invaders destroyed much of Baghdad in 1258?
questions.fact: Sadly, many precious books were lost, and the House of Wisdom was destroyed.

quests.title: Bronzes of Benin
quests.story: Behind huge earth walls lies the Oba's palace, shining with brass! Discover the West African Kingdom of Benin and its amazing artists.
quests.instruction: Read each question about Benin, then tap the right stone tablet.
quests.hint: Think about the Oba, his palace, and the skilled artists who worked in metal and ivory for him.

questions.ask: The Kingdom of Benin was in which modern country?
questions.fact: The modern country called Benin is a different place, a little to the west.

questions.ask: What was the king of Benin called?
questions.fact: There is still an Oba of Benin today, who is an important leader for the Edo people.

questions.ask: Which people built the Kingdom of Benin?
questions.fact: Benin City is the capital of Edo State in Nigeria today.

questions.ask: What huge structures surrounded Benin City and its lands?
questions.fact: Together the walls and ditches stretched for thousands of kilometres.

questions.ask: What were the famous 'Benin Bronzes' mostly made of?
questions.fact: Many are actually brass, a mix of copper and zinc, though we call them bronzes.

questions.ask: Which method did Benin's metal casters use?
questions.fact: A wax model was covered in clay, then the wax was melted out and metal poured in.

questions.ask: Who made the brass plaques and heads for the Oba?
questions.fact: The casters' guild lived and worked together in its own street in Benin City.

questions.ask: What did many of the brass plaques show?
questions.fact: The plaques decorated the pillars of the Oba's palace, recording ceremonies and events.

questions.ask: Which precious material from elephant tusks did Benin artists carve?
questions.fact: Ivory carvers made masks, bracelets and tall carved tusks for the Oba's altars.

questions.ask: Which European traders reached Benin in 1485?
questions.fact: They traded brass bracelets called manillas, which casters melted down to make art.

questions.ask: In 1897, soldiers from which country took thousands of artworks from Benin City?
questions.fact: Many of the objects ended up in museums in Britain and other countries.

questions.ask: What is happening to some Benin Bronzes today?
questions.fact: Since 2021, some museums and universities have returned bronzes to Nigeria.

quests.title: Where It All Began
quests.story: Four great civilisations grew up beside four great rivers, thousands of years ago! Pack each discovery into the right crate.
quests.instruction: Which civilisation is it from? Tap the right crate.
quests.hint: Match the river or invention to its land: Iraq, Pakistan and India, Egypt, or China.

questions.ask: Farms between the Tigris and Euphrates
questions.fact: This land between two rivers is called Mesopotamia.

questions.ask: Wedge-shaped cuneiform on clay tablets
questions.fact: Cuneiform is one of the oldest kinds of writing in the world.

questions.ask: Ziggurats, stepped temple towers
questions.fact: Each ziggurat had a shrine on top for the city's main god.

questions.ask: Grid streets with covered drains
questions.fact: Indus cities were carefully planned, with streets crossing at right angles.

questions.ask: The Great Bath at Mohenjo-daro
questions.fact: The Great Bath was waterproofed with a layer of tar called bitumen.

questions.ask: Square stone seals carved with animals
questions.fact: The seals carry a script that no one has been able to read yet.

questions.ask: Farms flooded each year by the Nile
questions.fact: The flood left rich black mud, so the Egyptians called their land Kemet, the black land.

questions.ask: Hieroglyphs written on papyrus
questions.fact: Papyrus was made from reeds that grew along the banks of the Nile.

questions.ask: Pyramid tombs for pharaohs
questions.fact: The Great Pyramid at Giza was the tallest building in the world for over 3,800 years.

questions.ask: Cities beside the Yellow River
questions.fact: The Yellow River gets its name from the yellow mud it carries.

questions.ask: Oracle bones with the first Chinese writing
questions.fact: Kings asked questions about the future, and the answers were carved on the bones.

questions.ask: Bronze vessels and woven silk
questions.fact: Shang bronze workers cast huge vessels using moulds made of clay.

quests.title: Scribes of Sumer
quests.story: In the shadow of a giant ziggurat, a scribe is pressing marks into wet clay. Join the scribe school and uncover the world's first cities!
quests.instruction: Read each question about Sumer, then tap the right tablet.
quests.hint: Think about life between two rivers, where clay and reeds were everywhere and cities were brand new.

questions.ask: Sumer was in Mesopotamia. Which country is most of Mesopotamia in today?
questions.fact: Mesopotamia means 'the land between the rivers' in ancient Greek.

questions.ask: Which two rivers flowed through the land of Sumer?
questions.fact: The rivers left rich mud on the land, which was good for growing crops.

questions.ask: What did Sumerian scribes write their cuneiform on?
questions.fact: Clay tablets baked hard in the sun or in fires, so thousands still survive.

questions.ask: What did scribes use to press marks into the clay?
questions.fact: The reed made wedge-shaped marks, and 'cuneiform' means 'wedge-shaped'.

questions.ask: What was most early Sumerian writing used for?
questions.fact: Scribes counted sheep, barley and taxes, so early writing was a bit like a list.

questions.ask: Which invention appeared in Mesopotamia around 3500 BC?
questions.fact: Some of the earliest wheels were potters' wheels, used for shaping clay pots.

questions.ask: What was a ziggurat?
questions.fact: The Great Ziggurat of Ur was built about 4,000 years ago, and parts still stand.

questions.ask: Which hero, a king of Uruk, stars in one of the world's oldest stories?
questions.fact: In the story, Gilgamesh goes on a quest to find the secret of living for ever.

questions.ask: The Sumerians counted in 60s. Where do we still use this today?
questions.fact: That's why there are 60 seconds in a minute and 60 minutes in an hour.

questions.ask: How did Sumerian farmers get river water to their fields?
questions.fact: Canals carried water to fields of barley, wheat and date palms.

questions.ask: Which board game was found in the royal tombs of Ur?
questions.fact: Experts worked out the rules from a later clay tablet, so people can still play it.

questions.ask: Which archaeologist dug up the royal tombs of Ur in the 1920s?
questions.fact: Woolley found gold jewellery, a golden helmet and beautiful lyres in the tombs.

quests.title: Indus City Planners
quests.story: Neat streets, matching bricks and drains under every road! Explore the brilliantly planned cities of the Indus Valley.
quests.instruction: Read each question about the Indus cities, then tap the right pot.
quests.hint: Think like a city planner: tidy streets, careful building, clean water and fair trade.

questions.ask: Roughly when did the Indus Valley civilisation flourish?
questions.fact: Its biggest cities were at their height from about 2600 to 1900 BC.

questions.ask: In which modern countries are the Indus Valley cities found?
questions.fact: The cities spread along the River Indus and other nearby rivers.

questions.ask: Which Indus city, rediscovered in the 1920s, has the Great Bath?
questions.fact: Mohenjo-daro may have been home to tens of thousands of people.

questions.ask: How were the streets of Indus cities laid out?
questions.fact: Main streets ran north to south and east to west, crossing at right angles.

questions.ask: What was special about the baked bricks used to build Indus cities?
questions.fact: Many bricks were in the same proportions, 4 to 2 to 1, for length, width and height.

questions.ask: What ran along the streets to carry dirty water away?
questions.fact: Drain covers could be lifted, so workers could clean the drains out.

questions.ask: What did many Indus houses have that was rare in the ancient world?
questions.fact: Waste water flowed from the houses into the street drains.

questions.ask: What was the Great Bath?
questions.fact: Historians think it may have been used for special washing ceremonies.

questions.ask: What did small square Indus seals often show?
questions.fact: The most common animal is a bull-like creature with one horn, like a unicorn.

questions.ask: What do we know about the writing found on Indus seals?
questions.fact: The inscriptions are very short, which makes the script hard to decode.

questions.ask: Which faraway civilisation did Indus merchants trade with?
questions.fact: Indus seals have been found in Mesopotamia, thousands of kilometres away.

questions.ask: What did Indus traders use to measure goods fairly?
questions.fact: The weights followed the same system across the whole civilisation.

quests.title: The Shang Oracle

skill.name: The Shang dynasty of ancient China
skill.subject: history

quests.story: The Shang king has a question for his ancestors, and the oracle bones are ready! Discover the bronze, jade and writing of ancient China.
quests.instruction: Read each question about the Shang, then tap the right torch.
quests.hint: Think about the Yellow River, the king's oracle bones and the skilled bronze and jade workers.

questions.ask: Roughly when did the Shang dynasty rule China?
questions.fact: The Shang are the earliest Chinese dynasty to leave written records.

questions.ask: Beside which river did the Shang build their cities?
questions.fact: The river is named after the yellow mud, called loess, that it carries.

questions.ask: What were oracle bones mostly made from?
questions.fact: Most were turtle shells or the shoulder blades of oxen.

questions.ask: How did diviners make cracks appear in oracle bones?
questions.fact: The king studied the cracks, and the question and answer were carved beside them.

questions.ask: Why are oracle bones so important to historians?
questions.fact: Some Chinese characters used today grew from the signs on oracle bones.

questions.ask: Near which modern city are the ruins of the last Shang capital, Yinxu?
questions.fact: Farmers there once dug up oracle bones and sold them as 'dragon bones' for medicine.

questions.ask: Which metal did Shang craftworkers cast into beautiful vessels?
questions.fact: Bronze is a mix of copper and tin, melted together and poured into clay moulds.

questions.ask: What was a ding?
questions.fact: Ding pots had three or four legs and were used in ceremonies for ancestors.

questions.ask: Who was Fu Hao?
questions.fact: Fu Hao was a wife of King Wu Ding and led his armies into battle.

questions.ask: When Fu Hao's tomb was found in 1976, what was inside?
questions.fact: It held over 700 jade objects and over 400 bronzes, and had never been robbed.

questions.ask: Which fine cloth was woven in Shang China?
questions.fact: Silk thread comes from the cocoons of silkworms, which feed on mulberry leaves.

questions.ask: Which two important jobs did the Shang king have?
questions.fact: The Shang believed their king could speak to the spirits of his ancestors.

quests.title: Battle of Britain Skies
quests.story: It is the summer of 1940, and the skies over southern England are full of planes. Find out how Britain was defended in the Battle of Britain.
quests.instruction: Read each question about the battle, then tap the right crate.
quests.hint: Think about the planes, the people on the ground who spotted enemy raids, and the pilots from many lands.

questions.ask: When was the Battle of Britain fought?
questions.fact: It was the first major battle fought almost entirely in the air.

questions.ask: Which air force defended Britain in the Battle of Britain?
questions.fact: RAF stands for Royal Air Force, which was formed in 1918.

questions.ask: What was the name of the German air force?
questions.fact: Germany hoped to beat the RAF so its army could cross the English Channel.

questions.ask: The Hurricane and which other famous fighter plane defended Britain?
questions.fact: Hurricanes actually shot down more enemy planes than Spitfires in the battle.

questions.ask: Which invention helped spot enemy planes long before they arrived?
questions.fact: The Chain Home radar stations along the coast could spot planes about 100 miles away.

questions.ask: Who watched and listened for planes once they had crossed the coast?
questions.fact: Volunteers watched the skies from posts all over the country, using binoculars.

questions.ask: What did WAAF plotters do in the RAF operations rooms?
questions.fact: WAAF stands for Women's Auxiliary Air Force; plotters tracked raids on huge table maps.

questions.ask: Where were RAF fighter planes kept, ready to take off?
questions.fact: Pilots waited near their planes, ready to 'scramble' into the air within minutes.

questions.ask: What name did Prime Minister Winston Churchill give the RAF pilots?
questions.fact: Churchill said that never had so much been owed by so many to so few.

questions.ask: Pilots from which country flew in the famous 303 Squadron?
questions.fact: Pilots also came from Czechoslovakia, Canada, New Zealand and many other countries.

questions.ask: Which date is remembered as Battle of Britain Day?
questions.fact: On that day in 1940 the RAF broke up two huge daytime raids over London.

questions.ask: What happened to Germany's plan to invade Britain after the battle?
questions.fact: Britain was not invaded, and the RAF pilots were remembered for their courage.

quests.title: Blitz Night

skill.name: The Home Front in the Second World War
skill.subject: history

quests.story: The siren is sounding over London, and families are heading for shelter. Sort the facts from the muddles about life on the Home Front.
quests.instruction: Is it true or false? Tap the right basket for each one.
quests.hint: Think about what kept people safe and fed at home: shelters, rationing, the blackout and growing food.

questions.ask: Families sheltered in Anderson shelters in their gardens
questions.fact: Anderson shelters were half buried in the ground and covered with earth.

questions.ask: London Underground stations were used as shelters
questions.fact: On some nights, over 150,000 people slept in Underground stations.

questions.ask: Evacuees wore name labels and carried gas masks
questions.fact: Evacuees were children sent from cities to the countryside to be safer.

questions.ask: Food rationing began in January 1940
questions.fact: Bacon, butter and sugar were among the first foods to be rationed.

questions.ask: ARP wardens checked that no lights showed at night
questions.fact: ARP stands for Air Raid Precautions; wardens also helped people find shelter.

questions.ask: Land Girls worked on farms to grow food
questions.fact: The Women's Land Army did farm work while many farm workers were away fighting.

questions.ask: Morrison shelters were built in back gardens
questions.fact: Morrison shelters were indoors: a strong steel cage that could be used as a table.

questions.ask: Evacuees were sent from the countryside to big cities
questions.fact: It was the other way round: children left the cities, where bombing was worst.

questions.ask: Sweets were never rationed during the war
questions.fact: Sweets were rationed from 1942, and rationing did not end until 1953.

questions.ask: In the blackout, windows had to be brightly lit
questions.fact: Thick blackout curtains kept every light hidden so bombers could not see towns.

questions.ask: Dig for Victory asked people to dig tunnels
questions.fact: Dig for Victory asked people to grow vegetables in gardens, parks and allotments.

questions.ask: The Blitz lasted for just one night
questions.fact: The Blitz lasted from September 1940 to May 1941, about eight months.

quests.title: The Historian's Toolkit
quests.story: The museum has new objects to catalogue, and every historian needs to know their sources! Decide which came from the time and which were made later.
quests.instruction: Made at the time, or later? Tap the right book for each one.
quests.hint: Ask: was this made or used by someone who was there at the time, or made later by someone looking back?

questions.ask: Samuel Pepys's diary from 1666
questions.fact: Pepys wrote about the Great Fire of London as it happened, and even buried his cheese!

questions.ask: A coin made in Roman times
questions.fact: Roman coins show emperors' faces, which helps historians date other finds.

questions.ask: A ration book from 1940
questions.fact: Ration books had coupons that shopkeepers marked or cut out when food was bought.

questions.ask: A photograph taken in Victorian times
questions.fact: Victorians had to keep very still for photographs, so few people are smiling.

questions.ask: A brooch worn by a Viking
questions.fact: Viking women often wore a pair of oval brooches to fasten their clothes.

questions.ask: A letter home from a soldier at the front
questions.fact: Letters show us how people felt, not just what happened.

questions.ask: A history textbook
questions.fact: Textbook writers study many primary sources and explain them for us.

questions.ask: A museum information board
questions.fact: Museum boards are written by experts today to explain the objects on display.

questions.ask: A documentary made this year
questions.fact: Documentaries often show primary sources, but the programme itself is made later.

questions.ask: A website about the Romans
questions.fact: Good historians check who wrote a website and where its facts came from.

questions.ask: A modern painting of the Battle of Hastings
questions.fact: A modern artist imagines the scene; the Bayeux Tapestry was made much closer to the time.

questions.ask: An encyclopaedia entry
questions.fact: Encyclopaedias collect what historians have found out into short summaries.

quests.title: The Grand Timeline

skill.name: Putting key events in history in order
skill.subject: history

quests.story: The museum's grand timeline has fallen off the wall! Rebuild 5,000 years of history, from Stonehenge to the Moon.
quests.instruction: Tap the event that happened longest ago, then the next one.
quests.hint: BC dates count down towards AD 1, and bigger BC numbers are longer ago. AD dates count up.

events.label: Stonehenge begun
events.fact: The first stage was a circular ditch and bank; the giant stones came later.

events.label: Great Pyramid built
events.fact: The Great Pyramid at Giza was built as a tomb for the pharaoh Khufu.

events.label: Shang dynasty begins
events.fact: The Shang ruled beside the Yellow River in China for over 500 years.

events.label: First Olympic Games
events.fact: The first recorded Olympic Games, at Olympia in Greece, had just one race.

events.label: Romans invade Britain
events.fact: Emperor Claudius sent about 40,000 soldiers, and Britain became part of the Roman Empire.

events.label: Baghdad founded
events.fact: Caliph al-Mansur built the Round City, which became a great centre of learning.

events.label: Battle of Hastings
events.fact: William of Normandy beat King Harold and became king of England.

events.label: Great Fire of London
events.fact: The fire began in a bakery on Pudding Lane and burned for four days.

events.label: Victoria crowned
events.fact: Victoria became queen in 1837, aged 18, and was crowned the next year.

events.label: Moon landing
events.fact: Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin were the first people to walk on the Moon.
